interactive.title: The winch and its energy ledger
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: The picture runs over fourteen small screens. The main picture is a motor winch on a frame. Its drum winds a rope that lifts a load on a hook. A height scale beside it runs from 0 to 10 m. Dragging the load sets its mass, from 100 to 1000 kg in 50 kg steps. It opens at 500 kg. Dragging a speed handle sets the hoist speed, from 0.1 to 0.5 m/s in 0.05 m/s steps. It opens at 0.2 m/s. On Lift, the load rises 10 m at that steady speed. At a steady speed the forces on the load balance. So the rope pulls up with the load's weight, its mass × 9.81 N/kg. For 500 kg that is 4905 N. Three bars show power: the electrical power in, the losses, and the power into the load. The power into the load is the rope's force × the speed. At the opening settings that is 4905 × 0.2 = 981 W. The winch is an example 80% efficient. So the electrical power in is 981 ÷ 0.8 = 1226 W. The other 245 W is losses. Readouts give the power into the load in W, the electrical power in in W, and the energy stored in the load in kJ. On a narrow phone the three readouts wrap onto two lines. The energy stored is the work done so far. It is the rope's force × the height risen. For 500 kg at 10 m it reads 4905 × 10 = 49,050 J. That is 49.05 kJ. Below the winch, a graph plots the energy stored against time. Its slope is the power. Its time axis runs from 0 to 120 s at every speed, so a faster lift draws a steeper line. The power bars keep one scale at every speed too, so a faster lift draws a longer bar. For 500 kg at 0.2 m/s the line reaches 49.05 kJ at 50 s. A Same lift, half speed button runs the lift again at half the speed. It draws a second line beside the first. Its bars are half as long, with the efficiency held at 80%. For 500 kg that is 490.5 W into the load and 613 W in. Its line rises half as steeply and reaches the same 49.05 kJ at 100 s. On this screen the time axis runs to 240 s. A Brake off button lets the raised load fall freely. The load falls freely, with the drum and motor's spin left out. The picture pauses after a 1 m fall and says so. A potential energy bar shrinks by the weight × 1 m, 4905 J for 500 kg. A kinetic energy bar grows by the same amount. That energy of motion is ½ × the mass × the speed squared. So the load is moving at √(2 × 9.81 × 1) = 4.43 m/s. The mass cancels, so any load reaches that speed in a free 1 m fall. The total energy stays the same. On a narrow phone the buttons wrap onto two lines too. Screen 1 lifts the opening 500 kg load 10 m: 4905 N × 10 m = 49,050 J. It says work is the area under a force-distance graph, and one joule is one newton moved through one metre. The stored energy is called potential energy. Screen 2 asks for the work done by a 200 N pull at 30° to the floor. The pull drags a crate 5 m along the floor. The answer is 866 J, from 200 × cos 30° × 5. One wrong pick is 1000 J, the whole pull × 5 m. The other is 500 J, from sin 30° instead of cos 30°. Screen 3 shows the power: 49,050 J ÷ 50 s = 981 W. So does 4905 N × 0.2 m/s. Screen 4 asks for the power to lift 200 kg through 5 m in 20 s. Its weight is 1962 N and the work is 9810 J. So the power is 490.5 W. One wrong pick is 9810 W, the work called a power. The other is 196,200 W, the work × the time. Screen 5 plays Same lift, half speed. Screen 6 asks what changes when the same load is lifted the same height at half the speed. The right pick is the same energy at half the power. One wrong pick is half the energy at the same power. The other is half the energy at half the power. Screen 7 shows the three bars and the efficiency. Efficiency is useful power out ÷ power in: 981 ÷ 1226 = 80%. Screen 8 asks for the efficiency of a winch that draws 800 W and puts 600 W into its load. The answer is 75%. One wrong pick is 133%, the power in ÷ the power out. The other is 25%, the 200 W of losses ÷ the power in. Screen 9 plays Brake off. It names the energy of motion kinetic energy. Screen 10 asks how fast a 200 kg load is moving after a free fall of 0.8 m. The answer is 3.96 m/s, from √(2 × 9.81 × 0.8). One wrong pick is 15.7 m/s, which is 2 × 9.81 × 0.8 with no square root. The other is 2.80 m/s, which leaves out the 2. Screen 11 shows a chain block. Pulling 30 m of hand chain with 250 N raises a 500 kg load 1 m. The work in is 250 × 30 = 7500 J. The work out is 4905 × 1 = 4905 J. So it is 4905 ÷ 7500 = 65.4% efficient. The other 2595 J is lost to friction. Its mechanical advantage is the load ÷ the effort, 4905 ÷ 250 = 19.62. Its velocity ratio is the effort's distance ÷ the load's, which is 30. Regrouped, (load × lift) ÷ (effort × chain) is (load ÷ effort) ÷ (chain ÷ lift). So 19.62 ÷ 30 gives the same 65.4%. Screen 12 asks for the efficiency of another chain block. There, 200 N on the hand chain raises 250 kg, and 20 m of chain lifts it 1 m. The answer is 61.3%. The weight is 2452.5 N. So the mechanical advantage is 2452.5 ÷ 200 = 12.26. Then 12.26 ÷ 20 is 61.3%. One wrong pick is 163%, the velocity ratio ÷ the mechanical advantage. The other is 6.25%, from the mass instead of the weight. Screens 13 and 14 mix it all. Screen 13 asks for the power going into a 500 kg load rising steadily at 0.2 m/s. The answer is 981 W. One wrong pick is 10 W, which is really the load's energy of motion in joules, ½ × 500 × 0.2². The other is 100 W, the mass × the speed with no 9.81. Screen 14 asks how much work a spanner does on a seized bolt. It applies a moment of 50 N m and the bolt does not turn. The answer is 0 J. The wrong picks are 50 J and 50 W. A moment is in newton metres too. But nothing moved, so no work was done. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers, with the right one in different places. A wrong pick is drawn so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The rope and drum are drawn with no mass. The rope does not stretch. The winch's efficiency is held at an example 80% at every load and speed. A real motor's efficiency changes with its load and speed. So a real half-speed lift draws more or less than half. The start and the stop are left out. Getting 500 kg up to 0.2 m/s takes only ½ × 500 × 0.2² = 10 J. That is tiny next to 49,050 J. Brake off lets the load fall freely, with no air drag and no drum to spin. A real drum and motor turn with the load and take some of that energy. So a real load would fall slower. The picture pauses after 1 m. A real falling load keeps speeding up until something stops it.

explain.text:
Work is a force moved through a distance. Power is how fast that work is done. So a slow lift puts the same energy into a load as a quick one. It does it at a lower power, for longer. Picture a motor winch lifting a 500 kg load at a steady 0.2 m/s. At a steady speed the forces on the load balance, as Newton's laws say. So the rope pulls up with the load's weight, 500 × 9.81 = 4905 N. A force does [[work]] when it moves something. The work measures the energy moved.[^1] It is the force times the distance moved along the force. On a graph of force against distance, the work is the area under the line. Only the part of a force along the movement counts. The dot product of the force and the movement picks out that part. Lift the load 10 m and the rope does 4905 × 10 = 49,050 J of work. That is 49.05 kJ. One joule is the work of one newton moving something one metre.[^2] So a joule is a newton-metre. That energy has not vanished. It is stored in the raised load, ready to come back. The work to raise it was its weight, mg, times its height, h. So the stored energy is mgh, called its potential energy.

[[Power]] is the work done per unit of time. That is the same as the energy moved per unit of time.[^3] One joule each second is one watt. At 0.2 m/s the 10 m lift takes 50 s. So the power into the load is 49,050 ÷ 50 = 981 W. A steady pull gives a shortcut. Each second the load rises 0.2 m. In that second the rope does 4905 × 0.2 = 981 J. So power = force × speed. Now lift the same load at 0.1 m/s. The force is the same weight. The height is the same 10 m. So the work is the same 49.05 kJ. Only the time changes. It doubles to 100 s, so the power halves to 490.5 W. Work says how much energy moves. Power says how fast it moves.

The motor takes electrical power from the supply. For a DC motor that is volts × amps. The motor loses some of it as heat on the way. The fraction that reaches the load is the winch's [[efficiency]]: useful power out ÷ power in. Say this winch is 80% efficient. To put 981 W into the load, it draws 981 ÷ 0.8 = 1226 W. The other 245 W becomes heat. A chain block keeps the same ledger by hand. Its efficiency is the work out ÷ the work in. That is the load × its distance over the effort × its distance. Regroup it into two ratios. The load ÷ the effort is its mechanical advantage. The effort's distance ÷ the load's distance is its velocity ratio. The efficiency is the mechanical advantage over the velocity ratio.

Let the brake off and the stored energy comes back as speed. Take a body speeded up from rest by a steady net force F over a distance s. Newton's second law gives F = ma. The slope and area of a speed-time graph give v² = u² + 2as, here with u = 0. So the work F × s = ma × s = ½mv². That is the energy of its motion, called kinetic energy. In a free fall the force is the weight, so mgh = ½mv². Fall 1 m, and the load's weight does 4905 × 1 = 4905 J of work on it. The load then reaches √(2 × 9.81 × 1) = 4.43 m/s. Energy is never made or destroyed. It is only moved or changed in form. The losses are energy too, carried off as heat. This winch is simplified. Its rope and drum are light, and its efficiency is fixed. A real winch's drum takes some energy to spin. Its efficiency changes with load and speed. **Work is force × distance and power is work ÷ time, so the same lift done at half the speed puts the same energy into the load at half the power.**[^3]

analogy.text: Think of two heaters on one energy meter. A 2 kW heater left on for 1 hour adds 2 kWh to the meter. So does a 1 kW heater left on for 2 hours. The energy is the same. The power is half and the time is twice as long. A winch does the same when it lifts the same load the same height at half the speed. It moves the same joules at half the watts, over twice the time.
analogy.breaks: A heater's energy ends as heat spread through the room. That heat is very hard to get back as electricity. Most of a winch's work stays in the raised load as stored energy. It comes back as speed when the brake comes off.

practice.text:
- Safe way first: a raised load is stored energy, held up by the brake. Never stand under it. A 500 kg load that drops freely for just 1 m arrives at 4.43 m/s carrying 4905 J.
- Find the force. For a steady lift it is the load's weight, its mass × 9.81 N/kg.
- Work = force × distance moved along the force, in joules.
- Power = work ÷ time, in watts. For a steady pull it is also force × speed.
- To find the power the motor draws, divide the power into the load by the efficiency.
- Check the size against the winch's rating.

**Rule of thumb:** each 100 kg lifted at 1 m/s takes about 1 kW at the load. The working is 100 × 9.81 × 1 = 981 W. Half the speed means half the power for the same energy.

**Worked example:** a winch lifts a 300 kg motor 6 m in 30 s. Take it as an example 75% efficient. The weight is 300 × 9.81 = 2943 N. The work is 2943 × 6 = 17,658 J, about 17.7 kJ. The speed is 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2 m/s. So the power into the load is 2943 × 0.2 = 588.6 W. The winch draws 588.6 ÷ 0.75 = 784.8 W. The other 196.2 W becomes heat. On an example 220 V DC supply that is 784.8 ÷ 220 = 3.6 A. That is a small winch, under 1 kW. Check it against its rating.

**Common mistakes**
- Calling work a power, or power a work. Work is in joules. Power is joules per second, which is watts.
- Working out ½mv² when asked for a steady lift's power. At a steady speed the energy of motion does not change. So all the power into the load goes into height.
- Using the mass in kg as the force. The force is the weight, the mass × 9.81.
- Writing newton meter for the unit. A newton meter is a spring balance that reads force. A joule is a newton-metre, a newton moved through a metre.
- Counting a moment as work. A moment is measured in newton metres too.[^4] A bolt that does not turn has had no work done on it.
- Forgetting the losses. The supply gives more than the load gets.

interactive.html:
A motor winch lifts a load 10 m. The height, the 80% efficiency and the puzzles' numbers are all examples.

Work is force × distance. Power is work ÷ time, which for a steady pull is force × speed.
interactive.title: The winch and its energy ledger
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the power bars halve while the energy stored ends at the same 49.05 kJ in twice the time, when you halve the hoist speed for the same 10 m lift.

checks.label: Work is the measure of energy transfer when a force moves an object through a distance: at every load and every height risen, the energy stored is the rope's pull × the height
One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a movement of one metre, so the lift's joules are its newtons × its metres
Power is work done per unit of time: at every load and speed, the power into the load is the energy stored at the top ÷ the time the lift takes
A moment is measured in newton metres, but it is not work: the bolt puzzle gives its moment in N m, and a bolt that does not turn has no work done on it
The opening lift: 500 kg weighs 4905 N; at 0.2 m/s 981 W goes into the load and 1226 W is drawn, so 245 W is lost; 10 m stores 49.05 kJ, in 50 s
Same lift, half speed: both power readings halve, to 490.5 W and 613 W, and the same 49.05 kJ is stored in 100 s, twice the time
Brake off: a 1 m free fall turns the weight × 1 m into motion, 4905 J for 500 kg, and reaches 4.43 m/s whatever the mass
Efficiency is useful power out ÷ power in: 80% at every load and speed, and the power-in bar is drawn exactly as long as the load and losses bars end to end
Every puzzle answer is worked from its rule (866 J, 490.5 W, 75%, 3.96 m/s, 61.3%, 981 W, 0 J), and the chain block is 65.4% both ways
Each puzzle offers three answers and accepts only its right one; every wrong answer has its own hint and its working drawn in red, and nothing is marked before Check
Every demonstration ends within 5 s of its screen opening, and every answer is drawn within 2.5 s of Check
Every screen that shows an idea says it in 90 words or fewer

applied.problem: The 981 W, 49,050 J, 50 s, 490.5 W, 613 W and 4905 J figures hold only at the opening 500 kg and 0.2 m/s, yet mass runs 100 to 1000 kg and speed 0.1 to 0.5 m/s; each must be tied to the opening settings.

"a little more or less than half" and "fall a little slower" overstate certainty: a motor's efficiency can fall well at light load, and a geared motor's spinning parts can take much of a falling load's energy.
"held only by the brake" is absolute (gearboxes and load brakes also hold loads), and "The size check passes" claims a pass against a rating the example never gives.
